chapters.name: Chapter 1: Setting up a clean dairy

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Choosing dairy cows and goats
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose dairy animals that fit your feed, money and market.
This lesson builds toward: Given your land, money, fodder and market, you will choose dairy cows or goats and lay out a zero-grazing unit with stall, feed trough, water and drainage, naming at least four checks you made before buying.
A dairy animal is only as good as the feed and care you can give it. A high-yielding Friesian (Holstein) cow needs a lot of good feed and water every day; if you cannot supply it, a cross with a local breed, or a smaller breed such as a Jersey or Ayrshire, may earn you more. In drier areas, hardy local breeds and crosses, such as zebu crosses in northern Nigeria or the Azawak zebu in Niger and Burkina Faso, cope better with heat and poor fodder.
Dairy goats suit small plots and smaller budgets. They eat less, cost less, and goat milk has its own buyers. In Kenya, Saanen, Toggenburg and Alpine goats and their crosses with local goats are kept for milk.
Before you buy, check: Do you have fodder and water all year, including the dry season? Who will buy your milk, and at what price? Can you reach a vet and an artificial insemination (AI) service? Then check the animal: buy from a known farmer with records, look for a healthy, alert animal with a well-shaped udder and four (cow) or two (goat) working teats, ask about past milk yield, calving and illness, and ask a vet or animal health officer to check her before you pay.
Step by step:
- List your fodder and water for the wet and dry seasons.
- Find your buyer and the price per litre.
- Find your nearest vet and AI service.
- Choose the breed or cross your feed can support.
- Buy from a known seller with records; check udder, teats and health.
- Ask a vet to examine the animal before you pay.
Words to know:
- Dairy breed: a breed raised mainly for milk, such as Friesian, Jersey or Ayrshire cows, or Saanen and Toggenburg goats.
- Cross: an animal whose parents are two different breeds, often an exotic dairy breed and a local breed.
- Artificial insemination (AI): putting semen from a chosen bull or buck into the female, done by a trained technician.
Official sources:
- ILRI: Smallholder dairy farmer training manual (Goopy and Gakige, ILRI Manual 24, 2nd edition, 2019)
Try it now: Write your own buying checklist: your fodder and water for the dry season, your buyer and price, your nearest vet and AI service, the breed or cross you can feed, and five things you will check on the animal before you pay.
You can now match a dairy breed to your feed and market and check an animal properly before you buy it.

check.q: You have little fodder in the dry season. Which choice is wisest?
options: Buy the highest-yielding Friesian you can find
Buy a cross or smaller breed your feed can support
Buy more cows so some survive
Buy now and plan fodder later
check.why: A cow only gives what her feed allows; a cross or smaller breed fits limited fodder.

check.q: Which check should you do before you pay for a cow?
options: Ask a vet to examine her and look at her records
Ask the seller if she is good
check.why: A vet check and records show health, past yield and calving.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Zero-grazing housing and feeding for milk
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Lay out a zero-grazing unit and plan feed and water for milk.
This lesson builds toward: Given your land, money, fodder and market, you will choose dairy cows or goats and lay out a zero-grazing unit with stall, feed trough, water and drainage, naming at least four checks you made before buying.
In zero-grazing, the animals stay in a unit and you bring feed to them, such as cut Napier grass, other fodder and crop residues. It saves land and lets you control feed, but it needs daily labour and good hygiene.
A good unit has: a roof for shade and rain; a stall or cubicle for each cow with dry, soft bedding so she can lie down; a floor that slopes so urine and water drain away; a feed trough and a water trough that are easy to clean; a clean, separate place to milk; a calf pen; a manure pit away from the milking area; and a store for feed. For goats, a raised slatted floor keeps them dry. Clean dung out every day, because dirty bedding is a main cause of mastitis.
Milk is made from feed and water. A cow in milk needs plenty of clean water all day, good roughage, and extra energy, protein and minerals in balance; milk drops fast when water or feed runs short. How to build a ration from local feeds is taught in "Livestock Nutrition and Feed Formulation with Local Ingredients". Here, remember two things: record what each feed costs, because feed is usually your biggest cost, and change feeds slowly.
Step by step:
- Mark out a roofed unit on well-drained ground.
- Give each animal a stall with dry bedding and a sloped floor.
- Place feed and water troughs where they are easy to fill and clean.
- Add a clean milking place, a calf pen and a feed store.
- Put the manure pit away from milking and water.
- Clean out dung every day; record feed bought and its cost.
Words to know:
- Zero-grazing: keeping animals in a unit and bringing all their feed to them instead of letting them graze.
- Bedding: dry, soft material on the floor where animals lie, such as wood shavings, dry grass or sand.
- Roughage: bulky feed such as grass, fodder, hay and crop residues.
Official sources:
- ILRI: Smallholder dairy farmer training manual (Goopy and Gakige, ILRI Manual 24, 2nd edition, 2019)
Try it now: Draw a simple plan of your zero-grazing unit (or the one you will build): stalls, bedding, floor slope, feed trough, water trough, milking place, calf pen, feed store and manure pit. Mark one thing you will fix first.
You can now lay out a zero-grazing unit that keeps animals dry and clean and explain how feed and water turn into milk.

check.q: Why should the floor of a zero-grazing stall slope?
options: So the cow can slide out
So urine and water drain away and bedding stays dry
So feed rolls to the cow
check.why: A dry floor and bedding keep udders clean and lower mastitis.

check.q: Where should the manure pit be?
options: Away from the milking place and water
check.why: Manure near milking or water spreads dirt and germs into the milk.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: A clean milking routine
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Milk a cow or goat with a clean routine, step by step.
This lesson builds toward: At every milking, you will carry out a clean milking routine from preparing the milker and utensils to filtering and covering the milk, doing every step in order with no step skipped.
Germs get into milk from dirty hands, dirty udders, dirty containers and the air of a dirty shed. A fixed routine, done the same way at every milking, keeps them out. Milk at the same times every day, in a clean place, calmly: a frightened animal lets down less milk.
Use smooth metal containers (aluminium or stainless steel) that are easy to clean. Plastic jerricans scratch and hold dirt, and many buyers reject milk that comes in them. Wash containers after every use with clean water and detergent, rinse, and dry them upside down on a rack in the sun.
Milk healthy animals first and any sick or treated animal last. Keep milk from an animal treated with a drug separate and do not sell it until the withdrawal period on the product label, or given by your vet, has passed.
Step by step:
- Wear clean clothes; keep nails short; wash your hands with soap.
- Bring clean, dry metal containers, a strip cup and a filter or clean sieve.
- Tie or settle the animal calmly in the clean milking place.
- Wash the teats (and udder only if dirty) with clean warm water and dry them with a separate clean cloth or paper for each animal.
- Squirt the first milk from each teat into a strip cup and look for clots, flakes or watery milk.
- Milk quickly and fully with the whole hand, not by pulling with the fingers.
- Dip or spray the teats after milking if your vet advises it, and give feed so the animal stays standing for a while.
- Filter the milk, cover it, and start cooling it at once.
Words to know:
- Strip cup: a cup with a dark plate or cloth on top; the first squirts of milk show clots or flakes on it.
- Teat dip: a disinfectant liquid the teats are dipped in after milking to kill germs; use one your vet recommends, as the label says.
- Withdrawal period: the time after a drug is given when milk or meat must not be sold or eaten; it is written on the label or given by the vet.
Official sources:
- ILRI: Smallholder dairy farmer training manual (Goopy and Gakige, ILRI Manual 24, 2nd edition, 2019)
- FAO Dairy production and products: milk quality and testing
Try it now: Watch or do one milking on your farm and tick each step in this lesson. Write down every step that was missed and one change to make tomorrow, such as one drying cloth per animal or a metal can instead of a jerrican.
You can now milk a cow or goat with a clean routine that keeps germs out of the milk.

check.q: Why squirt the first milk into a strip cup?
options: To see clots or flakes that show mastitis
check.why: The strip cup shows abnormal milk early, before it mixes with good milk.

check.q: A cow was treated by the vet two days ago. What do you do with her milk?
options: Mix it with the rest; a little is fine
Sell it to a different buyer
Feed it to her own calf without asking
Keep it separate and do not sell it until the withdrawal period on the label or from the vet has passed
check.why: Drug residues make milk unsafe and buyers test for them; the label or vet gives the waiting time.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Mastitis: signs, prevention and the CMT
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Check an animal for mastitis and run a California Mastitis Test.
This lesson builds toward: Given a cow or goat in milk, you will check for the signs of mastitis and run a California Mastitis Test on each teat, recording the result for each quarter or half and calling the vet for any positive or sick animal.
Mastitis is an infection and swelling of the udder. It lowers milk yield and quality and is one of the costliest dairy diseases. Clinical mastitis shows: a hot, swollen or painful quarter; clots, flakes, watery or bloody milk; and sometimes fever and no appetite. Subclinical mastitis shows nothing you can see, but the animal gives less milk. That is why you test.
The California Mastitis Test (CMT) finds hidden mastitis on the farm. You need a four-cup paddle and CMT liquid (reagent). Milk a little from each teat into its own cup, add the same amount of reagent, swirl, and read it within seconds. Milk that stays liquid is normal. A gel, slime or clumps mean high cell counts, which point to mastitis in that quarter. The stronger the gel, the stronger the reaction. Do not test in the first days after calving, when results are naturally high. Goat milk can react more strongly even when healthy, so ask your vet how to read results for goats.
Prevent mastitis with clean, dry bedding, the clean milking routine, a teat dip if your vet advises, milking infected animals last, and treating only with your vet's advice. Never give antibiotics on your own: follow the vet and the label. Record every case and every treatment.
Step by step:
- Look and feel: each quarter for heat, swelling or pain.
- Check the first milk on the strip cup for clots, flakes or blood.
- For the CMT: discard the first squirts, then milk a little from each teat into its own cup.
- Tilt the paddle so the right amount stays; add the same amount of reagent.
- Swirl gently and read within seconds: liquid is normal, gel means a reaction.
- Record the result for each quarter or half.
- Call your vet for any clinical case or positive result; follow the vet and the label.
Words to know:
- Mastitis: infection and swelling of the udder that lowers milk yield and quality.
- Subclinical mastitis: mastitis with no visible signs; only a test like the CMT shows it.
- Quarter: one of the four parts of a cow's udder, each with its own teat.
- Reagent: the liquid used in a test that reacts with the milk.
Official sources:
- University of Missouri Extension: Using the California Mastitis Test (procedure and interpretation)
- FAO Dairy production and products: animal health (mastitis lowers milk yield and quality)
Try it now: Run a CMT on one cow or goat (borrow a paddle and reagent from your cooperative, vet or extension officer if you have none). Record the result for each quarter or half in your notebook, and write what you will do about any reaction.
You can now spot the signs of mastitis, run a CMT on each teat, record the result and know when to call the vet.

check.q: Your cow's milk looks normal, but her yield has dropped. What could find hidden mastitis?
options: Waiting until the milk shows clots
check.why: Subclinical mastitis has no visible signs; the CMT shows it.

check.q: In a CMT, one cup turns into a thick gel. What does this mean?
options: The test was done right and the quarter is healthy
A strong reaction in that quarter; record it and call the vet
check.why: A gel means a high cell count, a sign of mastitis in that quarter.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Cooling, handling and selling milk
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Cool and deliver milk that passes the buyer's quality tests.
This lesson builds toward: After milking, with or without a cooler, you will cool, store and deliver milk so it passes the buyer's quality tests, reaching the cooler or buyer within the time the buyer sets, with nothing added to the milk.
Fresh milk has natural defences that hold germs back for only about three to four hours after milking. FAO advises cooling it to 4 °C within that time to keep its quality. With no cooler, stand the covered metal can in cool, clean running or stored water in the shade, and get the milk to the collection centre's cooler quickly. Never leave milk in the sun.
Most smallholders sell to a dairy cooperative, a collection centre, a processor, or a small dairy (for example, mini-dairies in Burkina Faso buy milk from herders and farmers). At delivery, the buyer tests your milk. Common tests are: look and smell; the alcohol test and the clot-on-boiling test, which show milk that is turning sour; the lactometer, which shows milk with added water; and, at some processors, a test for drug residues. Milk that fails is rejected or paid less.
Never add water, flour, preservatives or anything else to milk: it is cheating, it is often illegal, and the tests catch it. Ask your buyer how they pay (per litre, sometimes with a bonus for quality or fat), when they pay (often monthly by bank or mobile money), and what deductions they make. Read any contract fully before you sign. Selling raw milk to the public may need a permit: in Kenya the Kenya Dairy Board licenses milk handlers, so check its rules or your country's dairy authority.
Step by step:
- Filter and cover the milk right after milking.
- Cool it at once: cooler, or the can standing in cool water in the shade.
- Deliver to the collection centre or buyer within the time they set.
- Watch the tests and ask for the results.
- Record litres delivered, any rejection and the reason.
- Check every payment against your delivery records.
Words to know:
- Lactometer: a floating meter that measures how heavy (dense) milk is; added water makes milk lighter.
- Alcohol test: mixing milk with alcohol; milk that is turning sour forms clots.
- Collection centre: a place where farmers deliver milk to be tested, cooled and sent to a processor.
Official sources:
- FAO Dairy production and products: milk preservation (cool to 4 °C within 3 to 4 hours of milking)
- FAO Dairy production and products: milk quality and testing
- Kenya Dairy Board (regulates the dairy industry; permits for milk handlers)
- Kenya Dairy Board: licensing requirements
Try it now: Visit or phone your nearest collection centre, cooperative or buyer. Ask: which tests they do, the latest time they accept milk, how and when they pay, and what deductions they make. Write the answers down and compare them with how you handle milk now.
You can now cool and handle milk so it keeps its quality, explain the buyer's tests, and check how you are paid.

check.q: You have no milk cooler. What is the best thing to do after milking?
options: Stand the covered metal can in cool water in the shade and deliver quickly
Leave the milk in the sun to stay warm
Add a little water to keep it fresh
Keep it until tomorrow and deliver both milkings together
check.why: Cooling quickly and delivering fast keeps germs from multiplying.

check.q: What does the lactometer test at the collection centre catch?
check.why: Added water makes milk less dense, which the lactometer shows.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Calf rearing, records and cost per litre
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Calculate your cost per litre and keep the records that feed it.
This lesson builds toward: Given one month of farm records, you will calculate the cost per litre of milk and compare it with the price your buyer pays, with every cost included and the arithmetic correct.
Your calves and kids are your future herd. Make sure the newborn drinks colostrum, the first thick milk, as soon as possible after birth, ideally within the first few hours, because it carries the mother's protection against disease. Keep calves in a clean, dry, separate pen, give clean water, offer good hay or soft fodder and a calf feed early so the stomach develops, and wean when your extension officer or vet says the calf is eating enough solid feed. Follow your vet's plan for navel care, deworming and vaccination.
Keep simple records every day: litres per animal per milking, feed bought and its cost, heat signs and AI or service dates, calving dates, treatments with the date milk can be sold again, milk delivered, rejections and payments. A notebook works; a phone spreadsheet makes the sums easier.
Cost per litre = all costs in the month divided by litres produced. Example (figures are only an example): 3 cows in Kenya produce 1,050 litres in a month. Costs: feed and fodder KES 27,000, labour KES 9,000, vet and AI KES 3,000, other KES 3,000; total KES 42,000. Cost per litre = 42,000 / 1,050 = KES 40. If your buyer pays less than your cost per litre, you lose money on every litre; look first at feed waste, mastitis losses and rejected milk.
Step by step:
- Give colostrum as soon as possible after birth.
- Keep the calf in a clean, dry pen with water, hay and calf feed.
- Record litres, feed, breeding, calving, treatments, deliveries and payments.
- At month end, add up all costs.
- Divide total costs by litres produced: this is your cost per litre.
- Compare with the price paid and choose one change to lower the cost.
Words to know:
- Colostrum: the first thick, yellow milk after birth; it protects the newborn against disease.
- Weaning: moving a young animal from milk to solid feed.
- Cost per litre: all your dairy costs for a period divided by the litres you produced.
Official sources:
- ILRI: Smallholder dairy farmer training manual (Goopy and Gakige, ILRI Manual 24, 2nd edition, 2019)
Try it now: Final task: write your milking-hygiene routine to pin up in the milking area, then fill in a cost-per-litre sheet for last month (or an example month): every cost, the litres produced, the cost per litre, your buyer's price, and one change you will make.
You can now raise healthy calves, keep dairy records and calculate the cost of each litre of milk.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Animals and housing No link between the animals, the housing and the feed the farm has. The routine fits the farm's animals and unit: a clean milking place, dry bedding and manure kept away. Notes one housing fix with a date, such as better drainage or a separate milking place. Milking routine Steps are missing or out of order, for example no hand washing or no teat drying. All steps from milker and utensils to filtering, covering and cooling, in order. Says who does each step and how the routine is checked each week. Mastitis checks No mastitis signs or CMT in the routine, or home treatment without the vet. Lists the signs, when a CMT is done, how results are recorded, and calling the vet for positives; treated animals' milk kept out until the label or vet allows. Includes a simple CMT record table for each animal and quarter. Cooling and delivery Milk is left warm or delivered late; plastic containers used. Milk is cooled at once and delivered within the buyer's time, in metal containers, with nothing added. Records delivery times, test results and any rejection with its cause. Cost per litre Costs are missing or the sum is wrong. All costs listed, correct cost per litre, compared with the buyer's price. Names one change to lower the cost per litre and how its effect will be measured next month. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: When should a newborn calf drink colostrum?
options: As soon as possible after birth, ideally in the first few hours
check.why: Colostrum carries the mother's protection, and the calf takes it in best in the first hours.

check.q: Costs for the month are KES 36,000 and the cows produced 900 litres. What is the cost per litre?
